lead: A hot object does not glow equally at all wavelengths. Its spectrum has a peak, and the peak moves to shorter wavelengths as the object gets hotter. Classical physics could not explain this shape; its best formula predicted infinite energy at short wavelengths. In 1900 Planck fixed it by saying that the atoms in the hot body emit energy in small packets, or quanta, each of energy E = hν. This single idea started quantum mechanics, and the same curve is used today in pyrometry, star-temperature measurement and the cosmic microwave background.
prereq: You need: electromagnetic waves and intensity from Unit 3, and graph reading from Unit 2. The photon idea continues in 6.2.

sections.h3: The black body and its spectrum

blocks.text: A black body is an ideal absorber. It absorbs all radiation that falls on it and reflects nothing. The same object is also the best possible emitter at every wavelength. No real surface is perfect, but a small hole in a closed cavity kept at temperature T comes very close. Radiation that enters the hole bounces around inside and is absorbed before it can escape. The radiation that does escape is called cavity radiation, and its spectrum depends only on T, not on the wall material.

To record the spectrum, the escaping light is spread by a prism or grating, and the intensity per unit wavelength I(λ,T) is measured. I is power per unit area per unit wavelength, in W·m⁻² per m. At each T the curve is smooth: zero at λ = 0, a broad peak, and a long tail at large λ. As T rises, the whole curve rises and the peak moves to shorter λ.

blocks.where: λ<sub>max</sub> is the peak wavelength in m; T is the absolute temperature in K; the constant 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K is Wien's constant.

blocks.text: A 3000 K filament peaks at 966 nm, in the infrared. That is why an incandescent bulb heats a room more than it lights it.

Classical physics treats the cavity walls as charged oscillators and the radiation as waves. By equipartition, each mode of the field carries average energy kT, where k = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K is Boltzmann's constant. The number of modes per unit volume between ν and ν + dν grows as 8πν²/c³, so the energy density is u(ν) = (8πν²/c³) kT.

In wavelength language this becomes the Rayleigh-Jeans law: I(λ,T) ∝ T/λ⁴. At long λ it agrees with experiment. At short λ it fails badly: as λ → 0, 1/λ⁴ → ∞, so the predicted intensity and the total emitted energy both become infinite. This absurd prediction is the ultraviolet catastrophe. The name marks the short-wavelength end of the spectrum; the divergence appears even earlier, in the far ultraviolet and X-rays.

The fault lies in the assumption that an oscillator can take any energy, including zero. Every short-wavelength mode then receives the same share kT, and since there are ever more such modes, the sum never stops.

sections.h3: Planck's quanta and the radiation law

blocks.text: Planck's fix was one assumption. The oscillators in the wall cannot take any energy. Their allowed energies are E = n h ν, with n = 0, 1, 2, ... Here ν is the oscillator frequency in Hz, n is a whole number called the quantum number, and h is a new constant, the Planck constant: h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s. Energy changes only when n jumps, and each jump emits or absorbs one quantum of energy E = hν. The reduced constant is ℏ = h/2π = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.

blocks.where: E is the energy of one quantum in J; ν is frequency in Hz; λ is wavelength in m; h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s.

blocks.text: The average energy per mode is then not kT but hν ÷ (e<sup>hν/kT</sup> − 1). For long λ, hν is small compared with kT, and this reduces to kT, so classical physics is recovered. For short λ, hν ≫ kT, so the exponential is huge and the average energy is tiny. Short-wavelength modes are rarely excited, because one quantum of such a mode costs more energy than the thermal motion can supply.

blocks.where: I is the spectral radiance per unit wavelength; h is the Planck constant; c is the speed of light; λ is wavelength in m; k is the Boltzmann constant; T is temperature in K. The λ⁻⁵ factor counts modes; the exponential cuts them off at short λ.

blocks.text: The formula fits every measured curve with one constant h. Setting dI/dλ = 0 gives Wien's law; integrating over λ gives the T⁴ law, which is not derived here.

figure.caption: A hot cavity led classical physics to the Rayleigh-Jeans law and the ultraviolet catastrophe; Planck's energy quanta predicted the measured spectrum with its temperature-dependent peak.

spec.title: From black-body curve to Planck quanta
spec.aria: A downward flow from a hot body to the classical Rayleigh-Jeans law, its ultraviolet catastrophe at short wavelength, Planck's energy quanta, and the matched black-body spectrum.

examples.question: The surface of a star behaves as a black body at 6000 K. (a) Find the wavelength at which its spectrum peaks. (b) Find the frequency and the energy of one photon at that peak, in joules and in electron volts. Use b = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K, h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s and 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
steps: (b) Frequency at the peak: ν = c/λ<sub>max</sub> = (3.00 × 10⁸ m/s) ÷ (4.83 × 10⁻⁷ m) = 6.21 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
Photon energy: E = hν = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s) × (6.211 × 10¹⁴ Hz) = 4.12 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
In electron volts: E = (4.116 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) ÷ (1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J/eV) = 2.57 eV.
examples.check:
h = 6.626e-34
c = 3.00e8
T = 6000
b = 2.898e-3
lam = b / T
nu = c / lam
E = h * nu
eV = E / 1.602e-19
print(f'{lam:.2e}')
print(f'{nu:.2e}')
print(f'{E:.2e}')
print(f'{eV:.2f}')

traps: Using Wien's law to find total intensity. It gives only the peak wavelength; total emitted power needs the T⁴ law.
Forgetting units: b is in m·K, so T must be in kelvin and λ<sub>max</sub> comes out in metres, not nanometres.
Treating E = hν as a continuous classical energy. One quantum is hν, and a body emits in whole multiples nhν.
Swapping h and ℏ. h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s and ℏ = h/2π = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.
Thinking the peak shifts to longer wavelength as T rises. It shifts to shorter wavelength; the examiner's favourite graph asks you to mark this shift.

quiz.q: State Wien's displacement law and give the value of the constant with its unit.
quiz.a: λ<sub>max</sub> T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K, where λ<sub>max</sub> is the peak wavelength in m and T is the absolute temperature in K.

quiz.q: What is a black body, and what is a good practical approximation to it?
quiz.a: An ideal absorber that absorbs all incident radiation and reflects none; it is also the best emitter. A small hole in a heated closed cavity is a good approximation.

quiz.q: Why is the Rayleigh-Jeans prediction called the ultraviolet catastrophe?
quiz.a: It gives I(λ,T) ∝ T/λ⁴, which diverges as λ → 0. The predicted intensity and the total emitted energy both become infinite at short wavelengths, which experiment does not show.

quiz.q: In Planck's hypothesis, why do short-wavelength modes carry very little energy at a given temperature?
quiz.a: One quantum hν of such a mode is large compared with kT, so the average energy hν ÷ (e<sup>hν/kT</sup> − 1) is very small. The mode is rarely excited.

quiz.q: A black body is at 3000 K. Find its peak wavelength.
quiz.a: λ<sub>max</sub> = b/T = (2.898 × 10⁻³) ÷ 3000 = 9.66 × 10⁻⁷ m = 966 nm, in the near infrared.

quiz.q: Find the energy of one photon of wavelength 500 nm.
The Sun's spectrum peaks near 500 nm and the Earth's near 10 μm. Estimate the ratio of their surface temperatures.
quiz.a: Wien's law gives T ∝ 1/λ<sub>max</sub>. Ratio T<sub>Sun</sub>/T<sub>Earth</sub> = λ<sub>Earth</sub>/λ<sub>Sun</sub> = 10 μm ÷ 0.5 μm = 20. So the Sun's surface is about 20 times hotter.

quiz.q: Using the average energy per mode hν ÷ (e<sup>hν/kT</sup> − 1), explain why Planck's curve agrees with Rayleigh-Jeans at long wavelength and falls below it at short wavelength.
quiz.a: For small hν/kT, e<sup>hν/kT</sup> ≈ 1 + hν/kT, so the average energy tends to kT and the classical result is recovered. For large hν/kT, the average energy tends to hν e<sup>−hν/kT</sup>, which drops rapidly. Hence the curve matches at long λ and is cut off at short λ.

beyond: Not for the exam. The cosmic microwave background is the best black-body curve ever measured: it matches Planck's law at 2.725 K with a peak near 1 mm, which is why radio telescopes see it. Infrared pyrometers use the same curve to read furnace and steel temperatures without touching them. Thermal cameras and satellite radiometers calibrate against black-body cavities. Modern metrology uses h to define the kilogram, so Planck's constant now sits inside the International System of Units.
